opus-5.5.text:
I think what I loved about it was that it felt very concrete. In OI, a lot of the time the algorithm is fixed. Everyone knows the intended complexity, say O(n log n), and then the question becomes: can you make it actually run fast enough within the time limit? Sometimes your solution is right in theory but it's two or three times too slow, and that gap is where constant-factor optimization lives.

It was almost like a game with the machine. You start thinking about things the textbook doesn't care about: how memory is laid out, whether your accesses are cache-friendly, whether you can replace a division with a shift, unroll a loop, avoid recursion, use faster input reading, or restructure the data so the hot loop is tight. Each small trick gives you maybe ten or twenty percent, and then you stack them, and suddenly something that got TLE passes. That feedback loop is really satisfying, because you see the numbers go down right away.

I also liked that it forced me to understand what's really happening underneath. Big-O hides a lot. Once you start caring about constants, you realize that two "equivalent" solutions can differ by ten times in practice. That intuition stayed with me later, when I worked on systems and reinforcement learning infrastructure. A lot of that work is the same spirit: the algorithm might be standard, but making the environment simulation or the training pipeline fast is about finding the bottleneck, profiling, and squeezing out the overhead.

So for me it wasn't just a contest trick. It was kind of my first taste of engineering. Taking something that works and making it work really well.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So, constant-factor optimization — for people who don't know the OI world, that's when your algorithm already has the right big-O complexity, but it still times out, and you have to make it actually run fast. Shaving off that factor of two or three or ten.

What I enjoyed about it was that it's the part of the contest where theory ends and the machine starts talking back to you. Most of competitive programming is about the idea: find the right data structure, prove the complexity, done. But constant-factor work forces you to think about what's really happening underneath. Cache behavior, memory layout, whether your inner loop is branch-heavy, whether reading input with cin versus a hand-written fast reader costs you half a second. You start to feel the hardware.

I remember the first time I replaced a vector of structs with separate arrays, and a solution went from timing out to passing with room to spare. Nothing about the algorithm changed. That was a little revelation for me: the same math, but the way you arrange bytes in memory decides whether you win or lose. It felt almost like a hidden second game inside the contest.

There's also a craftsmanship aspect. It's very hands-on, very iterative. You measure, you try something, you measure again. Sometimes the "obviously faster" trick makes things slower, and you have to figure out why. I found that loop really satisfying because the feedback is immediate and honest. The judge doesn't care how elegant your reasoning was.

And honestly, that mindset carried over. Later, when I was working on systems for reinforcement learning and simulation, it was the same instinct: the algorithm is fine, so where is the time actually going? Profile it, look at the data movement, cut the waste. A lot of what people call "engineering" in ML is really constant-factor optimization at a much bigger scale. So OI was kind of where I learned to enjoy that.

It felt like a little puzzle within the bigger problem: where was the unnecessary work, and how much could you squeeze out of it? There was something very satisfying about getting more out of an approach you already understood.

You could have the right algorithm, but by changing the memory layout, avoiding unnecessary work, or making an inner loop tighter, you could make it noticeably faster. It felt like a puzzle within the puzzle: how much more performance could I squeeze out of the same idea?
